### Doctrinal Construction of Law & Reconstruction of Individual Sovereignty

Confronted with the complex threat of affective and subliminal manipulation, the positive doctrine of Civil Law must be fundamentally reconstructed to safeguard individual sovereignty in the digital age. Within the traditional Civil Law framework—particularly referencing the doctrine of Defects of Will / Vitiated Consent as enshrined in Article 1320 and Article 1328 of the Indonesian Civil Code (Burgerlijk Wetboek)—a contract is declared void ab initio or may be rescinded when there exists a element of Mistake / Error (*dwaling*), duress (*dwang*), or Fraud / Deceit (*bedrog*). However, these classical legal instruments were crafted for face‑to‑face or conventional correspondence transactions, where human awareness was presumed to be under full personal control. When a digital transaction or consent is mediated by persuasive algorithms that exploit subconscious vulnerabilities, the concepts of *dwaling* and *bedrog* must be broadened to encompass systemic, non‑transparent architectural manipulation (Hildebrandt, 2015).

This doctrinal reconstruction demands the application of strict liability to AI developers in cases where severe psychological, physical, or financial harm arises from synthetic empathy manipulation or systematically misleading outputs (Article 1365 of the Indonesian Civil Code (Burgerlijk Wetboek) in conjunction with the EU AI Act Regulation 2024/1689). Under this framework, it is unnecessary to prove personal mens rea; it suffices to demonstrate objectively that the product released to the public market possesses a structural defect that injures users’ cognitive autonomy (Weizenbaum, 1976). Just as motor‑vehicle manufacturers are strictly liable for brake failures regardless of intent, artificial‑intelligence developers must bear full responsibility for failures of cognitive‑safety mechanisms that precipitate mental collapse in their users (Jonas, 1979).

Furthermore, Article 5 of the EU AI Act imposes an absolute prohibition on AI systems that deploy subconscious techniques beyond an individual’s awareness to materially distort behavior in ways that cause—or are highly likely to cause—physical or psychological injury. This doctrine introduces a novel legal concept: the right to cognitive integrity as an inseparable component of universal human rights and personal data protection (Indonesian Personal Data Protection Act (Law No. 27/2022)). Individual sovereignty therefore extends beyond bodily integrity and data privacy to include an absolute right to preserve the space of consciousness from covert algorithmic interventions designed to erode freedom of thought (Farahany, 2023). States and international supervisory bodies now possess a legitimate legal basis to undertake preventive interventions, seize computational models proven to be manipulative, and impose crippling sanctions on corporations that trade human souls for algorithmic profit (Zuboff, 2019).

In synthesis, legal protection for citizens in the era of digital transformation requires a harmonious blend of stringent preventive regulation, victim‑oriented enforcement, and an adaptive overhaul of civil liability doctrine attuned to the realities of artificial intelligence. As the boundary between human and machine blurs under the onslaught of synthetic empathy and omnipotent latent‑space calculations, law must stand as the final bastion defending civilization. Individual sovereignty is not a relicary illusion of past jurisprudence; it is an ethical lighthouse that must be continuously upheld so that humanity is not reduced to mere objects of commodification within the global digital consciousness factory (Floridi, 2013).
